screens.title: Variables, Data Types, and Basic Operators
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will gain a practical understanding of three foundational ideas: variables as labeled containers for values, the core Python data types you will encounter first, and the basic operators that let you compute and change values. Variables let you give a meaningful name to a value so your program can read, update, and reuse that information. Data types tell Python what kind of value you have — whole numbers, decimal numbers, text, or truth values — and they determine what operations are valid. Operators like +, -, and * are the tools that act on those values and update variables using assignment forms such as equals and plus-equals. We’ll use short code samples to check types, show safe conversions between types, and reveal common pitfalls such as trying to convert an arbitrary string to a number. You’ll practice by calculating a simple total cost and inspecting types with the type function. By the end you should be able to explain what a variable is, pick an appropriate type, convert values safely, and use arithmetic and assignment operators without surprising results. Think about a recipe: ingredients are variables, each ingredient has a type, and operators are the steps that transform them. What ingredient will you name first in your program?

screens.title: What is a Variable?
screens.narratorSegment: A variable is a named place in a program where you store a value so your code can refer to it later. Think of a variable as a labeled box in memory: the label is the variable name and the contents are the value. This makes code readable because you describe what the value represents instead of repeating raw numbers or strings. In Python, creating a variable is a simple assignment: you name the box and use the equals sign to put a value inside. For example, age equals thirty stores the number thirty in the box labeled age. Because Python is dynamically typed, the same variable can be assigned different types over time, but good practice keeps a variable focused on a single kind of value to avoid confusion. A common beginner mistake is using reserved keywords as variable names; doing that will cause a syntax error and stop your program. Another frequent error is assuming assignment copies by value in ways that matter for mutable data — for simple types like integers and strings this is safe, but for compound objects you must be mindful. Practice by naming a few variables for a shopping item: item_name, item_price, and in_stock, then print them. How will naming your variables help someone else reading your program?

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › What is a Variable?
Core Concept
Variables as labeled boxes
Use variable names to describe data so code reads like a recipe. Clear names reduce bugs and make maintenance easier.
Analogy
A variable is like a labeled jar in a pantry. The label helps anyone pick the right ingredient when following a recipe.
Common mistake
Using reserved words like print as names or starting a name with a digit will produce syntax errors.
Key Takeaway
Name variables clearly and initialize them with meaningful values to make code self-explanatory.
Example assignments and inspection
# assign values
age = 30
user_name = "Cohortia"
price = 19.99
is_active = True

# inspect types
print(type(age))       # <class 'int'>
print(type(user_name)) # <class 'str'>
Run these lines to see each variable's type. Use descriptive names like user_name and item_price.

screens.title: Variable Naming Conventions
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing good variable names follows a short set of rules and a style recommendation that makes your code easier to read and less error-prone. The basic syntax rules are simple: a name must start with a letter or underscore, may contain letters, numbers, or underscores after that, and Python is case-sensitive so quantity and Quantity would be different names. Avoid using Python keywords as names because the interpreter treats them specially; trying to use a keyword as a name will raise a syntax error and stop your script. Style guidance from PEP 8 favors snake_case: all lower-case words with underscores between them. That style helps other Python developers read your code immediately. A practical habit is to make names descriptive but concise, like total_price or user_count. Watch out for names that accidentally shadow built-in functions — using list or str as a variable name hides the built-in behavior. Try this: create three valid snake_case names and one invalid name starting with a digit to see the error. Naming is not just pedantry; it prevents bugs and makes debugging much faster. Which naming habit will you adopt first?

keyIdea.title: Naming rules
keyIdea.text: Start with a letter or underscore, use snake_case for readability, and avoid keywords or built-ins as names.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Naming Conventions
Process
Rules and style steps for choosing names
Step 1 — Syntax rules
Start with a letter or underscore; follow with letters, numbers, or underscores; remember names are case-sensitive.
Step 2 — Avoid keywords
Do not use reserved Python keywords like if, for, or print as variable names; this will cause syntax errors.
Step 3 — Prefer snake_case
Use all lowercase with underscores to separate words for clarity and community consistency.
Step 4 — Avoid shadowing built-ins
Don't name variables list, str, or dict if you still need the built-in functionality later.
Examples and checks
# valid names
user_name = "Alex"
_total = 5
items_3 = 10

# invalid name (starts with digit) — causes SyntaxError
# 7_days = "week"
Try uncommenting the invalid line in a REPL to observe the syntax error. Rename variables to fix.
Key Takeaway

Clear, correct names reduce bugs and make code easier to read by others and yourself later.

screens.title: Core Data Types: int, float, str, bool
screens.narratorSegment: Python provides a small set of fundamental types that cover most simple programs: integers for whole numbers, floats for decimal numbers, strings for text, and booleans for truth values. Integers represent whole numbers and support standard arithmetic operations; they have no decimal part. Floats include fractional parts and are used when more precision or division results are needed. Strings are sequences of characters used to express text; they can be enclosed in single, double, or triple quotes for multi-line text. Booleans represent True or False and are essential for conditions and logic. Knowing a value’s type tells you what operations are valid: you can add two integers or concatenate two strings, but trying to add a string and an integer will raise a type-related error until you convert one side. Use the type function to inspect a value at runtime. Practice by creating examples for each type and printing type inspections. A common misconception is assuming that a numeric-looking string behaves like a number; it does not until explicitly converted. When you check types and convert responsibly, you avoid many runtime errors. Which type will you examine first?

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Core Data Types
Data Types
int • float • str • bool
Each type describes allowed operations and how values behave in expressions and assignments.
Integer (int)
Whole numbers without decimals. Example: 42
Float (float)
Numbers with a decimal point. Example: 3.14
String (str)
Text enclosed in quotes. Example: "Hello"
Boolean (bool)
Truth values True or False. Used in conditions.
Quick comparisons and behavior
Numeric vs Text
A numeric literal like 10 behaves differently than the string "10". To use "10" in math you must convert it to a numeric type first.
Boolean usage
Booleans control flow: comparisons produce booleans, and logical operators combine them for decision-making.
Try this example
a = 10
b = 3.5
name = "Python"
is_ready = True

print(type(a))   # <class 'int'>
print(type(b))   # <class 'float'>
print(type(name))# <class 'str'>
print(type(is_ready)) # <class 'bool'>
Run these lines and inspect each printed type. This helps connect the term to runtime behavior.

screens.title: Integers and Floats — Type Inspection and Behavior
screens.narratorSegment: When you run arithmetic with integers and floats, remember how Python chooses the result type. Division with a single slash always returns a float even when the operands are integers, while floor division discards the fractional part and returns an integer when dividing two integers. Use the type function to confirm the actual type returned by any expression. Try assigning a integer value to a variable and a float to another, then compute both regular division and floor division so you can observe the difference directly. For example, dividing ten by three yields a float with a fractional part; using floor division with double slash yields three, discarding remainder. A common misconception is expecting integer division to always return an integer when using the single slash. Modern Python returns a float for single slash. Use parentheses to control precedence and be explicit with casting when you need a specific type for later operations. Practice by computing expressions and printing both the value and its type so the result and type align with your expectations. What will happen if you divide a float by an int?

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Integers & Floats
Code Walkthrough
Division and type inspection
# integer and float division
x = 10
y = 3
z = 10.0

print(x / y)      # 3.333...
print(type(x / y))# <class 'float'>

print(x // y)     # 3
print(type(x // y))# <class 'int'>

print(z / y)      # 3.333...
print(type(z / y))# <class 'float'>
Run these lines to confirm when results are floats and when they are ints. Observe how float operands influence results.
Explanation cards
Division (/)
Always returns a float even for integer operands. Useful when fractional results matter.
Floor division (//)
Discards fractional part. Use when you explicitly need an integer quotient.
Check your understanding
If you divide a float by an int, the result is a float. Try print(type(10.0 / 3)).

screens.title: Strings and Concatenation
screens.narratorSegment: Strings represent text and are one of the most common types you'll use. You can use single or double quotes for short strings, and triple quotes for multi-line text. String concatenation uses the plus operator to join pieces of text, but remember that concatenation requires both operands to be strings. A frequent beginner error is attempting to add a number and a string directly. To combine text with numbers, convert the number to a string first or use formatted output. Strings are immutable in Python, so operations like concatenation create new string objects rather than modifying an existing one. Practice examples help cement the rules: create a name variable, a score variable as a number, then convert the number to a string before joining. Also try printing numeric values by converting them to strings to build clearer output messages. When you need both clarity and performance, prefer formatted strings for readability. How will you present mixed text and numbers in your next program? Strings and Concatenation means use quotes for strings, convert numbers before concatenation, and prefer formatted output for clarity.. In practical terms, how to represent text, use quotes, and combine strings safely. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Strings & Concatenation
Code Examples
Quotes, concatenation, and conversion
name = "Alex"
score = 95

# convert number to string before concatenation
message = "Player: " + name + ", Score: " + str(score)
print(message)

# formatted output alternative (readable)
print(f"Player: {name}, Score: {score}")
Try both methods; formatted strings keep code clean and avoid explicit conversions scattered through expressions.
Notes & pitfalls
Immutability
String operations return new strings; modifying many large strings can be less efficient than joining lists.
Type error example
Adding a number and string directly causes a TypeError. Convert or format instead.
Key Takeaway
Convert non-strings before concatenation or use formatted strings for clarity and correctness.

screens.title: Booleans and Comparison Operators
screens.narratorSegment: Booleans represent truth values and are central for decisions and control flow. Comparison operators such as equal, not equal, greater than, and less than produce boolean results that you can use in conditions. For example, comparing a numeric variable to a target returns True when the comparison holds and False otherwise. In Python booleans are capitalized True and False; using lowercase will not produce the boolean values Python expects. Logical operators like and, or, and not combine boolean expressions to form more complex conditions. A common misunderstanding is thinking booleans are only a separate type; in Python they are a subtype of integers in many contexts but should be treated semantically as truth values. Practice by evaluating a few comparisons and printing both the comparison result and its type. Also try combining comparisons with and and or to see when conditions become True. How might these comparisons determine the flow of a small program, such as deciding if a user has permission based on is_admin and has_permission? Booleans and Comparison Operators means comparisons return true or false; logical operators combine conditions to drive program decisions.. In practical terms, how comparisons produce booleans and why capitalization matters. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Booleans & Comparisons
Comparison Examples
Operators that produce booleans
a = 10
b = 3
print(a == 10)   # True
print(b > 5)   # False
print(a != b)    # True

# combining
is_admin = False
has_permission = True
print(is_admin and has_permission) # False
print(is_admin or has_permission)  # True
Run these lines to observe True or False results and use the type function to confirm boolean type.
Notes
True and False
Boolean literals must be capitalized. They are commonly produced by comparison expressions.
Common pitfall
Confusing assignment and comparison. Using a single equals is assignment, double equals compares values.
Check your understanding
Try print(type(a > b)) to confirm comparisons return booleans and drive conditional logic.

screens.title: Type Checking and Casting
screens.narratorSegment: Type checking and casting lets you inspect values and change their representation when necessary. Use the type function to discover a value’s type at runtime. When converting, int, float, and str are the primary tools: int converts numeric strings to integers where appropriate, float converts strings with decimals, and str turns numbers into text for display. Always validate input before casting because trying to convert a non-numeric string to an int or float raises a ValueError. For example, converting the string "123" to int yields the number one hundred twenty-three, but converting "hello" will fail. When reading user input from the console, remember it arrives as text, so convert it before arithmetic. Also be aware that int conversion truncates the decimal part rather than rounding. Practice by converting a numeric string and adding a number, then attempt an invalid conversion inside a try block in the REPL to see the error and learn defensive checks such as str. isdigit or try-except. Which conversion will you practice first? In practical terms, using type(), int(), float(), and str() with safe conversions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will gain a practical understanding of three foundational ideas: variables as labeled containers for values, the core Python data types you will encounter first, and the basic operators that let you compute and change values. Variables let you give a meaningful name to a value so your program can read, update, and reuse that information. Data types tell Python what kind of value you have — whole numbers, decimal numbers, text, or truth values — and they determine what operations are valid. Operators like +, -, and * are the tools that act on those values and update variables using assignment forms such as equals and plus-equals. We’ll use short code samples to check types, show safe conversions between types, and reveal common pitfalls such as trying to convert an arbitrary string to a number. You’ll practice by calculating a simple total cost and inspecting types with the type function. By the end you should be able to explain what a variable is, pick an appropriate type, convert values safely, and use arithmetic and assignment operators without surprising results. Think about a recipe: ingredients are variables, each ingredient has a type, and operators are the steps that transform them. What ingredient will you name first in your program?

By the end of this chapter you will be able to define what a variable is, choose names that follow Python conventions, identify and use the fundamental data types, check and convert types, and apply basic operators to compute and update values. First, you will explain variables as named storage and give a simple example like assigning 30 to a variable called age so the program can reuse that number. Next, you will follow naming rules such as starting with a letter or underscore and preferring snake_case for readability. You will also recognize int, float, str, and bool values when you see them, and use the type function to confirm a value’s type. You will practice safe type conversion with int, float, and str, and learn the common error that occurs when converting a non-numeric string. Finally, you will use arithmetic operators such as plus, minus, multiply, division and floor division, and assignment forms like plus-equals to update variables. Each objective includes a small practice or check so you can confirm competency as you learn. Which objective will you try first?

These objectives map to small, verifiable checks you can run quickly. For variables, create a named variable and print it to confirm the value. For naming, try creating three variables that follow snake_case and one intentionally invalid name to see the syntax error and learn from it. For data types, use the type function to inspect an integer, a float, a string, and a boolean so you can match visual examples to actual type output. For type conversion, convert a numeric string into an integer and use it in arithmetic; then attempt to convert a non-numeric string to see the ValueError and learn how to avoid it. For operators, compute a sum, a floor division, and an exponentiation example to notice the difference between slash division and double-slash floor division. Each check is small: run it, observe the printed output and the data type, then explain why the result matches the rules. These quick checks build confidence and reveal common beginner mistakes early.

A variable is a named place in a program where you store a value so your code can refer to it later. Think of a variable as a labeled box in memory: the label is the variable name and the contents are the value. This makes code readable because you describe what the value represents instead of repeating raw numbers or strings. In Python, creating a variable is a simple assignment: you name the box and use the equals sign to put a value inside. For example, age equals thirty stores the number thirty in the box labeled age. Because Python is dynamically typed, the same variable can be assigned different types over time, but good practice keeps a variable focused on a single kind of value to avoid confusion. A common beginner mistake is using reserved keywords as variable names; doing that will cause a syntax error and stop your program. Another frequent error is assuming assignment copies by value in ways that matter for mutable data — for simple types like integers and strings this is safe, but for compound objects you must be mindful. Practice by naming a few variables for a shopping item: item_name, item_price, and in_stock, then print them. How will naming your variables help someone else reading your program?

Choosing good variable names follows a short set of rules and a style recommendation that makes your code easier to read and less error-prone. The basic syntax rules are simple: a name must start with a letter or underscore, may contain letters, numbers, or underscores after that, and Python is case-sensitive so quantity and Quantity would be different names. Avoid using Python keywords as names because the interpreter treats them specially; trying to use a keyword as a name will raise a syntax error and stop your script. Style guidance from PEP 8 favors snake_case: all lower-case words with underscores between them. That style helps other Python developers read your code immediately. A practical habit is to make names descriptive but concise, like total_price or user_count. Watch out for names that accidentally shadow built-in functions — using list or str as a variable name hides the built-in behavior. Try this: create three valid snake_case names and one invalid name starting with a digit to see the error. Naming is not just pedantry; it prevents bugs and makes debugging much faster. Which naming habit will you adopt first?

Python provides a small set of fundamental types that cover most simple programs: integers for whole numbers, floats for decimal numbers, strings for text, and booleans for truth values. Integers represent whole numbers and support standard arithmetic operations; they have no decimal part. Floats include fractional parts and are used when more precision or division results are needed. Strings are sequences of characters used to express text; they can be enclosed in single, double, or triple quotes for multi-line text. Booleans represent True or False and are essential for conditions and logic. Knowing a value’s type tells you what operations are valid: you can add two integers or concatenate two strings, but trying to add a string and an integer will raise a type-related error until you convert one side. Use the type function to inspect a value at runtime. Practice by creating examples for each type and printing type inspections. A common misconception is assuming that a numeric-looking string behaves like a number; it does not until explicitly converted. When you check types and convert responsibly, you avoid many runtime errors. Which type will you examine first?

When you run arithmetic with integers and floats, remember how Python chooses the result type. Division with a single slash always returns a float even when the operands are integers, while floor division discards the fractional part and returns an integer when dividing two integers. Use the type function to confirm the actual type returned by any expression. Try assigning a integer value to a variable and a float to another, then compute both regular division and floor division so you can observe the difference directly. For example, dividing ten by three yields a float with a fractional part; using floor division with double slash yields three, discarding remainder. A common misconception is expecting integer division to always return an integer when using the single slash. Modern Python returns a float for single slash. Use parentheses to control precedence and be explicit with casting when you need a specific type for later operations. Practice by computing expressions and printing both the value and its type so the result and type align with your expectations. What will happen if you divide a float by an int?

Strings represent text and are one of the most common types you'll use. You can use single or double quotes for short strings, and triple quotes for multi-line text. String concatenation uses the plus operator to join pieces of text, but remember that concatenation requires both operands to be strings. A frequent beginner error is attempting to add a number and a string directly. To combine text with numbers, convert the number to a string first or use formatted output. Strings are immutable in Python, so operations like concatenation create new string objects rather than modifying an existing one. Practice examples help cement the rules: create a name variable, a score variable as a number, then convert the number to a string before joining. Also try printing numeric values by converting them to strings to build clearer output messages. When you need both clarity and performance, prefer formatted strings for readability. How will you present mixed text and numbers in your next program? This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Booleans represent truth values and are central for decisions and control flow. Comparison operators such as equal, not equal, greater than, and less than produce boolean results that you can use in conditions. For example, comparing a numeric variable to a target returns True when the comparison holds and False otherwise.
